description: The convoy of the locomotive 15 operated by Mr. Tito is located in hopper OP2 positioning the 1st car under the hopper, the assistant does not observe anything out of the ordinary (dry load there is no presence of water) and initiates the chute, for this, the hydraulic module of the hopper is switched on and with the controls it slightly moves the hopper handle and an untimely flow of water and mud splashes the operator generating the described injury, in addition the collaborator was 7 meters from the line of fire
sif_reason: This event describes a classic and well-documented high-severity mining hazard: an unexpected release of water and mud from a hopper/chute during unloading. The pre-task inspection found the load to be dry with no presence of water, yet an "untimely flow of water and mud" occurred once the chute was opened — indicating trapped/hidden water or saturated material behind a dry crust that was not detectable by visual inspection alone. This is the same underlying mechanism as "mud rushes" or "uncontrolled draw point releases," which are recognized in the mining industry as capable of causing serious injury, entrapment, or fatality due to the force, volume, and speed of material release. Critically, the operator was struck by the splash from 7 meters away, which indicates the release carried significant energy/force — not a gentle drip or seep. The explicit mention that the collaborator was in the "line of fire" at that distance reinforces that this was a hazard zone with a genuine escalation pathway, and the actual outcome (a splash injury) reflects a fortunate variation of an event that could plausibly have been far more severe (e.g., higher volume/pressure release, closer proximity, or being caught in the flow path).

hazard_notes: Hydraulic/gravitational — uncontrolled, unexpected release of pressurized/trapped water and mud from a rail hopper chute during unloading operations; hidden hazardous energy not identified by standard pre-task visual inspection
consequence_notes: Under a worse-case variation of this same event (larger volume of trapped water/mud, higher pressure/force behind the material, closer proximity to the discharge point, or the operator being positioned directly in the flow path rather than at the edge of it), this could plausibly result in being knocked down, struck with significant force, entrapment/burial in mud, or being swept/pulled toward the discharge opening — outcomes consistent with serious injury or fatality; the fact that a splash reached and injured someone 7 meters away indicates the release carried more force than a routine, controlled discharge
barrier_notes: Failed — the pre-task visual inspection ("dry load, no presence of water") did not detect the hazard, indicating this inspection method is inadequate for identifying trapped/hidden water or saturated material in this type of load; no indication of remote/controlled chute activation procedures, standoff barriers, or a validated line-of-fire exclusion zone that accounted for this failure mode
exposure_notes: Operator positioned within the hopper's "line of fire" (discharge trajectory zone) at a distance of 7 meters during chute activation; direct exposure to the projected water/mud flow despite this stand-off distance

description: In circumstance, the AHK-903 license plate (Empresa which serves the supervision of CMA, carried out the field inspections in the upper bank 4288, when unexpectedly when climbing through the operational access (positive ramp), It slides in an excavated area of ​​approximately 3 meters high, remaining in position with the front part on the floor. sif_reason: This event involves a vehicle losing traction/control while climbing an operational access ramp and sliding into an excavated area approximately 3 meters deep, coming to rest with its front end down. This combines two high-energy hazard mechanisms: (1) loss of vehicle control on an incline (positive ramp), and (2) a fall/drop of ~3 meters into an excavation. Either mechanism alone is a recognized SIF-category hazard in mining (vehicle rollover/loss of control, and falls from height/into excavations). The vehicle ending in a nose-down position at the bottom of a 3m drop indicates substantial uncontrolled energy was involved. The fact that occupants were using seatbelts and full PPE appears to be the key factor that prevented serious injury — meaning this reads as a near-miss / high-potential event where the controls worked, not a low-energy incident.
